Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify the bearing surface characteristics of modern metal-on-metal articulations.
Recognize appropriate surgical candidates and contraindications to hip resurfacing.
Compare technical considerations that may optimize outcomes of hip resurfacing.
Evaluate the survivorship and clinical outcomes of hip resurfacing in vivo.
Review common complications of hip resurfacing.
Explain the pathophysiology of adverse local tissue reaction (ALTR).

Metal-on-metal articulations result in less volumetric wear than metal-on-polyethylene
articulations.
This decreased wear may reduce the incidence of osteolysis-induced failure.
Enthusiasm for the use of metal-on-metal articulations is tempered by concerns for the
generation of metal ion debris compared with standard metal-on-polyethylene or ceramic
bearing surfaces.
Metal-on-Metal Lubrication Theory
The wear characteristics of metal-on-metal prostheses generally are characterized by a run-in
wear rate that usually occurs in the first 1 million cycles and is followed by a uniform rate of
wear.
The overall volume of wear of metal-on-metal prosthetic joint surfaces has been related to the
presence of a minimum elastohydrodynamic fluid film thickness for the mean operating
conditions of load, speed, viscosity, and elastic properties of the metals used in each
prosthesis, which is described by the lambda ratio.
The lambda ratio is the ratio of the thickness of the fluid film to the composite root mean
square surface roughness.
If the lambda ratio is 1 or less for a metal-on-metal bearing, severe mixed lubrication
conditions occur, which means that abrasive wear occurs via direct contact of the two bearing
surfaces. A lambda ratio of 3 or higher indicates that fluid film lubrication is sufficient to
substantially reduce the effect of load and, therefore, minimizes friction and wear.
Lower clearance and larger femoral head sizes promote higher lambda ratios.
In total hip arthroplasty (THA), clearance is the difference between the diameter of the
femoral head and the diameter of the acetabular cup, with clearances of 100 to 200
μm maximizing fluid film thickness. These clearances maximize joint fluid entrapment
between the two bearing surfaces.
Clearances that are too high result in increased wear, and clearances that are too low may
result in clamping and/or equatorial seizing.
A larger femoral head diameter increases the entrainment velocity (ie, the speed with which
the fluid is brought into the joint), maximizing fluid film lubrication. Even with an ideal head
diameter and clearance, mixed film lubrication likely occurs most frequently in vivo.
Contact patch–to–rim (CPR) distance
CPR distance is the distance between the point of application of the joint reaction force and
the rim of the acetabular implant in a patient in a standing position.

An inverse relationship exists between wear and CPR distance.
A CPR distance of less than 5 mm is associated with increased metal ion levels and increased
rates of prosthetic loosening, wear, and dislocation.
Factors that result in decreased CPR distance include a high abduction angle of the acetabular
implant, excessive anteversion of the acetabular cup, and cup designs with smaller arcs of
coverage of the femoral head.
In Vivo Results
Early in vivo data from an analysis of retrieved McKee–Farrar prostheses showed mean linear
wear rates of 0.003 and 0.004 mm/year for the femoral head and cup, respectively. Larger
diameter (42 mm) femoral heads had a twofold lower mean volumetric wear rate than smaller
diameter (35 mm) femoral heads (0.7 versus 1.4 mm3 per year, respectively).1
Current-generation metal-on-metal bearings (high-carbon, wrought cobalt-chromium alloy)
with a 28-mm-diameter femoral head had a mean in vivo wear rate of 27.8 μm/year for the
first year of use and 6.2 μm/year after the second year, with femoral heads generally
exhibiting a higher wear rate than acetabular cups. A positive correlation was observed
between clearance and wear rate.
Metal-on-metal bearings and corresponding metallic wear debris can release metallic ions in
substantially greater concentrations than that which typically occurs with polyethylene-
covered or ceramic bearings, and these ions may form soluble or precipitated organometallic
substances.
Metal-on-metal wear debris particles are approximately 10 to 50 nm.
Corrosion, mechanical and chemical, of the articular surfaces of a metal-on-metal joint
prosthesis leads to the production of metal ions (eg, Co2+), which are measured in the tissues,
blood, and urine. The concentrations of these ions currently with resurfacing and stem-type
hip devices are being measured prospectively and have been found to be increased in all
series in which they have been measured.
Disadvantages of Metal Bearings
Recently, two types of adverse reactions have been noted in failed metal-on-metal THA
implants that produced osteolytic responses with persistent pain, the frequency of which is
unknown.

One such adverse reaction is a perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes indicative of a delayed-
type hypersensitivity response to metal wear products, with the development of a typical
immunologic response.
Other studies have noted the presence of plasma cells, B lymphocytes, and massive fibrin
exudation not characteristic of a Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction and
described as an aseptic, lymphocyte-dominated, vasculitis-associated lesion (ALVAL) or as a
lymphocyte-dominated immunologic answer.2

Disadvantages of Metal Bearings
Pseudotumors or ALTRs have been described after metal-on-metal hip resurfacing and
with THA implants that have a large femoral head, with a substantially higher incidence
in the latter group. The histopathology of several retrieved pseudotumors has been
consistent with aseptic, lymphocyte-dominated, vasculitis-associated lesions in
combination with substantial tissue necrosis. Pseudotumor has been reported in both
painful and well-functioning prostheses; however, the degree of implant wear has not
yet been directly correlated with the severity of ALTRs.
Metal wear particles generated by metal-on-metal THA may have cytotoxic effects
because of the dispersal of these particles throughout the body.
An early review on the incidence of cancer in patients with prostheses with metal-on-
metal bearings found that leukemia was the only cancer that may occur at an increased
rate in these patients. The follow-up period was 5 to 14 years; however, longer follow-up
did not reveal any increased risk of hematopoietic cancers.3
More recent, large population-based studies have shown no greater risk of
hematopoietic or other cancers at 7-year follow-up.4
Importantly, a 20-year follow-up study of patients who underwent THA did not show a
difference in the mortality rate between patients with a metal-on-metal hip and those
with a metal-on-polyethylene hip.5

Hip Resurfacing Arthroplasty
Indications
Ideal candidates are relatively young, active male patients with advanced osteoarthritis6

Indications
The theoretic advantages of hip resurfacing arthroplasty (HRA) include proximal femur
bone preservation, low wear rate, and high range of motion to impingement driven by
an increased jump distance with a large-diameter femoral head. These advantages must
be balanced against concerns regarding the biologic effect of metal ions and the
increased risk of femoral neck fracture, which may result in early failure. Therefore, the
decision to perform HRA over traditional THA must be made after consideration of risks
and advantages. In general, younger male patients with a larger femoral head and
denser bone structure will better benefit from the advantages of HRA and have a lower
risk for complication relative to other patient populations (Resource 1).
Contraindications
Absolute Contraindications
Females of childbearing age
Serum level increases in metal ions are not considered to be safe in pregnancy; therefore,
HRA must be avoided in this patient population.
Metal allergy
Patients with a documented metal allergy may be at an increased risk of adverse reaction to
metal ion debris. 
Renal failure
Metal ions released from bearing surfaces are largely cleared through the kidneys; therefore,
renal failure results in increased serum ion levels, specifically cobalt and chromium, which
may be associated with an increased risk of toxicity.2
Relative Contraindications

Poor bone quality: dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan less than −1.0.
Severe deformity of the femoral head and neck
Severe post–Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease or slipped capital femoral epiphysis deformity: These
may be a relative contraindication to HRA if realignment of the femoral implant with the native
neck would create bony defects.3
Severe cystic changes in femoral neck or head/osteonecrosis: Large bone cysts (>1 cm) in the
femoral neck or head or a substantial area of femoral head osteonecrosis may compromise
cemented fixation or predispose to fracture.

Contraindications
The most common complication of HRA is femoral neck fracture. Because low bone
density substantially increases the risk of fracture, THA is the preferred technique for
this patient population.
Because HRA involves retention of the native femoral neck, the technique does not allow
for correction of any substantial proximal femur deformity, such as increased femoral
anteversion in patients with hip dysplasia.
Hip Dysplasia

Hip Dysplasia
Frequently, dysplastic hips lack sufficient acetabular bone stock and often are associated
with proximal femur deformity with increased anteversion. Because the acetabular
component is monoblock without screw fixation, bony support for the implant may be
inadequate. In addition, dysplasia is more common in females and may predispose
patients to advanced arthritis at a young age.
Femoral Head Size
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:16 AM
AAOS | Alternative Implant Designs: Hip Resurfacing
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004018
6/23


Femoral Head Size
Evidence suggests that patients with smaller bone structure, defined as a head diameter
of less than 50 mm, have an increased risk of poor outcomes after HRA. The only FDA-
approved HRA implant currently available starts at size 48.
Surgical Technique

Surgical Technique
Numerous surgical approaches can be used for HRA. Compared with traditional THA,
some modifications to the standard approach are necessary to ensure adequate
visualization, access, and protection of vascularity. Dissimilar from traditional THA, HRA
requires complete exposure of the head/neck junction, which necessitates a
circumferential capsulotomy. This allows the femoral head to be adequately elevated for
femoral preparation and allows for increased translation of the femur to allow for
acetabular preparation (Video 1).
Video 1

Moroni A, Micera G, Miscione MT, Orsini R: Video. Surgical Technique: Hip Resurfacing
Postero-Lateral Approach. Bologna, Italy, 2016.
Modified Posterior Approach
Release of the upper portion of the gluteus maximus tendon
Preservation of femoral neck soft tissues and circumferential capsulotomy

Modified Posterior Approach
Release of the upper portion of the gluteus maximus insertion on the linea aspera
facilitates adequate mobilization of the femur and avoids undue compression of the
sciatic nerve as the hip is dislocated. This is repaired during closure and does not affect
postoperative rehabilitation or functional recovery.
With a posterior approach, the capsule is taken down from its attachment on the femur
as usual. Superiorly and anterosuperiorly, the capsule generally is released from its
attachment on the acetabulum with the use of capsular scissors.
In addition, care must be taken to protect the vascularity of the femoral neck via
preservation of the soft-tissue sleeve, which contains branches of the medial femoral
circumflex vessel. This can be achieved by avoiding the use of electrocautery directly on
the femoral neck, particularly at the inferior 6-o’clock position, which is the location at
which the inferior retinacular vessels enter to perfuse the femoral head.
Anterior Approach

Anterior Approach
Anterior capsulectomy and circumferential capsulotomy are performed to achieve
adequate femoral exposure. Release of the tensor fascia lata origin proximally may be

Sizing the Femoral Head

Sizing the Femoral Head
If between sizes, the best option is to size up to avoid notching of the femoral neck4
(Video 2).
Video 2
Su EP: Video. Measuring the Femoral Head. New York, NY, 2021.
Retraction of the Femur, Reaming of the Acetabulum, and Placement of the Cup

Retraction of the Femur, Reaming of the Acetabulum, and
Placement of the Cup
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:16 AM
AAOS | Alternative Implant Designs: Hip Resurfacing
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004018
9/23

Offset reamers and cup inserters facilitate this portion of the procedure. Some surgeons
prefer to prepare the femur first because this may reduce the bulk of the femoral head
and ease retraction and visualization during preparation of the acetabulum. The
advantages of a femur-first approach must be balanced against concerns for retractor-
induced damage to the prepared femoral head with exposed cancellous bone.
The importance of cup positioning has been clearly established in traditional THA and
HRA. In HRA, the importance of achieving an appropriate inclination of approximately
40° is paramount because increasing inclination is associated with edge loading,
increased wear, and a higher risk for ALTR and associated failure. Lack of modularity and
increased stiffness of the cobalt-chromium acetabular components increase the
challenge of properly seating the component because the floor cannot be visualized
through screw holes. In addition, achieving a satisfactory anteversion angle may be more
complex because HRA does not allow for substantial changes in femoral version;
therefore, the effect of cup positioning on combined anteversion must be assessed and
will vary based on individual patient anatomy.5

Femoral Head Preparation
Preparation of the femoral head is shown in Video 4.7
Placement of the femoral neck pin and confirmation of appropriate positioning
Overdrilling of the pin and insertion of the cannula to guide the femoral preparation
Sequential preparation of the femur with the use of cylindrical, flat, and chamfer reamers

Appropriate pin placement is vitally important for the ensuing steps of femoral preparation.
Target pin alignment should be coaxial to the native femoral neck or slightly valgus. Varus
placement predisposes patients to femoral neck fracture, and excessive valgus will increase the
risk of notching during cylindrical reaming. A stylus is used to assess clearance after the pin is
placed. The tip of the stylus should not contact the neck. If inadequate clearance of unsatisfactory
alignment is noted, the pin position must be revised before preparation is completed.
The cylindrical portion of femoral head preparation should be in neutral or slight valgus
alignment relative to the native femoral neck. Care must be taken to avoid notching of the
femoral neck during this portion of the procedure.
Cementation of the Femoral Component

Cementation of the Femoral Component
SEND FEEDBACK

A drill is used to prepare pock marks around the chamfer and on the flat surface of the
medial head to optimize surface area for cement interdigitation and fixation. The use of
proximal femoral suction through a cannula in the trochanter may further improve
interdigitation. The goal of cementation is relatively uniform cement penetration of 2 to
5 mm, full seating of the component, and avoidance of excessive impaction force that
may increase the risk of fracture.5

satisfactory midterm results: the Birmingham Hip Resurfacing System (Smith & Nephew)
and the Conserve Plus Implant (Wright Medical Technology). Of these, only the
Birmingham Hip Resurfacing System remains on the market1,8,9,18-20 (Table 1).

Daniel et al8 reported 15-year overall implant survivorship of 95.8%; however,
substantial differences were observed between males (98%) and females (91.5%). In
addition, patients with a primary diagnosis of osteoarthritis had better survivorship
(99.4%) than those with a diagnosis of osteonecrosis or hip dysplasia. Other studies have
reported lower survivorship, with Amstutz et al9 noting a Kaplan-Meier survivorship rate
of 88.5% at a follow-up of 10 years. Femoral head size greater than 46 mm and the
absence of cysts over 1 cm were protective, with no failures occurring in these patients.

Complications
Femoral Neck Fracture

Femoral Neck Fracture
Femoral neck fracture is a unique complication of HRA compared with traditional THA
because of preservation of the native femoral neck. Similar to fractures of the native hip,
the femoral neck is an anatomic area predisposed to fracture. This may be because of
postoperative biomechanical considerations and/or biologic/vascular factors.
In a multicenter registry study in Australia, the incidence of femoral neck fracture after
hip resurfacing was approximately 1.5%.10 However, several large series by experienced
surgeons have estimated the rate to be lower than 1%.11 This suggests that femoral neck
fracture may be related to surgical technique, such as femoral implant positioning, bone
preparation, and blood supply preservation. Higher-volume surgeons may have greater
experience in avoiding technical factors that may predispose patients to femoral neck
fracture.
Femoral neck fractures typically occur within the first 3 months postoperatively. Patient
factors include osteopenia, overuse, and trauma. After a femoral neck fracture occurs,
revision surgery is necessary. Typically, the femoral neck fracture will be displaced,
requiring conversion to an endoprosthetic stemmed device. If the existing hip
resurfacing socket is well fixed and positioned, then a matching dual-mobility ball can be
used. Otherwise, the socket can be revised, and a traditional THA socket with the bearing
of choice can be inserted.
Notching

Notching
Notching of the femoral neck may occur during preparation of bone for the femoral
resurfacing implant. During the course of bone preparation, a sharp, cylindrical reamer
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:16 AM
AAOS | Alternative Implant Designs: Hip Resurfacing
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004018
16/23

is used over a guidepost placed in the femoral neck. The goal is to prepare the femoral
head so that the cylindrical portion is in a neutral to slight valgus position relative to the
femoral neck. If the cylindrical reamer teeth come into contact with the femoral neck,
then a notch is said to have occurred. In general, notching will occur on the anterior and
superior aspects of the femoral neck because of the location at which the reamer exits
the bone.
Notching theoretically predisposes the femoral neck to fracture. Other factors, such as
the size and strength of the native bone, play a role. Notching of the femoral neck noted
intraoperatively does not necessarily mean that resurfacing cannot be continued; rather,
protected–weight bearing may be advisable.
Adverse Local Tissue Reaction

Adverse Local Tissue Reaction
ALTR, also called adverse reaction to metal debris, is an immunologic response to the
cobalt and chromium particles created by the articulation. Histologic studies originally
identified this response in the synovial tissues about failed metal-on-metal total hip
implants.12 Findings included a proliferation of small vessels with a predominance of
lymphocytes, and researchers hypothesized a type IV (lymphocyte-mediated)
hypersensitivity. They termed the finding aseptic, lymphocyte-dominated, vasculitis-
associated lesion, which remains a histologic diagnosis. The true incidence of ALTR is
unknown because some patients may not have clinical manifestations; however, long-
term follow-up studies clearly show that the incidence is higher in women compared to
men.26
Pathophysiology

Pathophysiology
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:16 AM
AAOS | Alternative Implant Designs: Hip Resurfacing
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004018
17/23

ALTR is characterized by joint effusion and synovial hypertrophy about the metal-on-
metal articulation. It may represent a phagocytic response to a large amount of metal
debris and/or an immunologic reaction to a normal amount of debris. If this process
continues chronically, osteolysis; enlargement of lymph nodes; and involvement of
adjacent muscles, nerves, and blood vessels are possible.
Clinical Manifestations

Clinical Manifestations
Clinically, patients typically feel a sensation of swelling, clicking, or popping within the
joint. Low-grade aching and pain may be present. Often, this pain refers to the groin and
the lateral hip/bursal area. A limp or abductor weakness is a concern for muscle
involvement.
Workup

Workup
Standard AP and lateral radiographs should be evaluated for osteolysis, radiolucency, or
neck narrowing. Evaluation of a HRA implant for ALTR also should include the
measurement of blood metal ion levels of cobalt and chromium. Although no cutoff
blood metal ion levels exist in the United States, the Medicines and Healthcare Products
Regulatory Agency of the United Kingdom has set an upper limit of 7 parts per billion for
cobalt and 7 parts per billion for chromium.13 In numerous studies, well-functioning HRA
implants are associated with metal ion levels ranging from 2 to 3 ppb.14 Therefore, metal
ion levels higher than this may warrant close monitoring. Higher metal ion levels indicate
articular surface wear, and the excessive generation of metal particles may cause ALTR
via the normal physiologic response of phagocytosis; however, low metal ion levels do
not preclude the possibility of ALTR because it can occur via the immunologic
hypersensitivity mechanism.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:16 AM
AAOS | Alternative Implant Designs: Hip Resurfacing
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004018
18/23

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein levels also may be helpful in the
workup for ALTR. These measurements may be mildly elevated, indicating an
inflammatory host response; however, they also may indicate infection. Therefore, if
these markers are elevated, joint aspiration is indicated.
If any of the test results suggest ALTR (elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-
reactive protein level, metal ion level) or if the patient has clinical symptoms, then
advanced cross-sectional imaging is indicated. This may involve ultrasonography or MRI
with metal-artifact reduction sequencing. At some institutions, a special kind of MRI with
multi-acquisition variable-resonance image combination is even more sensitive in
detecting ALTR.15 Nawabi et al16 demonstrated that multi-acquisition variable-resonance
image combination MRI was 90% sensitive in detecting intraoperative tissue damage
about a metal-on-metal THA implant. At other institutions, ultrasonography was more
readily available; investigators have reported similar success using ultrasonography to
screen for fluid and soft-tissue abnormalities.15
Management

Management
Management of ALTR consists of revision surgery, in which the tissue response is excised
via a complete synovectomy and the implants are removed so the production of metal
debris is eliminated. Typically, both components are revised and a THA implant inserted.
If the resurfacing acetabular component is well fixed and well positioned, retention is
considered. Retention of the acetabular component may reduce the morbidity
associated with component removal and accelerate recovery because immediate–weight
bearing is permitted. A stemmed THA femoral implant, with a polyethylene dual-mobility
bearing, can be used to match the existing acetabular implant. Blevins et al17 reported
that this technique resulted in good outcomes in most patients, reducing the risk of
failed ingrowth of a newly implanted acetabular component.
By eliminating the production of metal debris from the bearing, metal levels diminish to
the point of normalization and the clinical symptoms of ALTR are expected to resolve.

Rare cases in which the soft-tissue reaction persists have been described, and the
process of revision and synovectomy must be repeated; however, this has not the
experience of the authors of this lesson.
